package main

import "fmt"

func main() {
	p := new([3]int)
	p[1] = 4
	fmt.Println(p[1])
	fmt.Println(len(p[:]))
}

package main

import "fmt"

func main() {
	x := 3
	p := &x
	pp := &p
	qq := pp
	**qq = 8
	fmt.Println(x)
}

package main

import "fmt"

func main() {
	x, y := 1, 2
	p := &x
	pp := &p
	*pp = &y
	**pp = 9
	fmt.Println(x)
	fmt.Println(y)
}

package main

import "fmt"

func main() {
	x := 2
	p := &x
	pp := &p
	fmt.Println(**pp)
}
What is the bridge between *T and another *U?
Why does uintptr not keep an object alive for GC?
options: uintptr always points into the stack
It is an integer, not a pointer: the collector does not scan it

questions.text: When is converting uintptr back to unsafe.Pointer defined?
options: Immediately in the same expression, without parking a bare address across a call that may let GC move the object

questions.text: Why would a function take **T?
options: To replace the caller’s pointer, not the object behind it
Otherwise you cannot change T’s fields

questions.text: Why can you not compare a struct with a []byte field, but you can compare two *S?
options: Pointers compare addresses, not contents; a slice field makes T incomparable

questions.text: What does i == j compare when both any values hold *T?
options: The dynamic type and pointer identity

questions.text: Why is reflect.ValueOf(x).CanSet() false, while ValueOf(&x).Elem() is often true?
options: Elem always panics on a pointer
ValueOf(x) is a copy; a pointer’s Elem refers to the original variable

questions.text: What does the method value t.add bind when add has a pointer receiver?
options: A pointer to t; later writes to t are visible
A copy of t at creation time
Nothing: it is only the method name
An interface holding a typed nil

questions.text: What does the method value t.get bind when get has a value receiver?
options: A copy of t at creation time

questions.text: What does atomic.Pointer[T] add over a plain *T?
options: Atomic Store/Load/CAS without a race on the pointer itself

questions.text: Why does the promoted field o.n panic when Outer embeds a nil *Inner?
options: It dereferences the nil Inner pointer

questions.text: Does Go have dangling pointers to a finished stack frame?
options: No: escape analysis moves the variable to the heap
Yes if you return &x from a goroutine

questions.text: What happens on i.(*T) when i holds a typed nil *T?
options: ok is true, the value is a nil *T
ok is true and an empty interface

questions.text: Why are two any values holding (*int)(nil) and (*string)(nil) unequal?
options: nil is never equal to nil

questions.text: What does assigning a T (not *T) to an interface copy?
options: A pointer to the original variable
Nothing; the interface refers to the stack
A copy of T into the interface; later mutations touch only that copy

questions.text: Why convert uintptr back to unsafe.Pointer in the same Offsetof expression?
options: So the address does not live as an integer across GC safe points
uintptr cannot be added to Offsetof

questions.text: Can you compare two *S values when S has an incomparable field?
options: Yes: you compare addresses, not S

questions.text: What does reflect.New(t) do?
options: Returns a nil pointer of type t
Allocates a zero value and returns a Value of a pointer to it
Panics if t is not a struct

questions.text: What does swap(a, b **int) change?
options: Which pointer variables point where, not the int values

questions.text: Why does (*int)(unsafe.Pointer(&a)) work for type A int?
options: Same layout; unsafe.Pointer strips the type
A and int are the same type to the compiler
GC converts A to int by itself

Embedding a nil *Inner makes reading a promoted field a safe zero.
Adding uintptr and Offsetof should stay in one expression that converts back to a pointer.

CompareAndSwap on atomic.Pointer compares addresses, not *T.

Which type bridges different *T and *U?
Why must you not park an address in uintptr?
questions.answer: GC does not treat uintptr as a pointer and may move the object.
